subtitle: A feudatory king between sword and silence

panels.shot: dramatic split-scene wide, half battlefield and half ascetic hall, seen from a slight low angle
panels.action: Marasimha II Satyavakya stands at the center, one side of him armored amid a dusty Rashtrakuta war-camp, the other draped in plain cloth seated on a stone platform in a Jain shrine, his face calm and unreadable.

dialogue.text: He won wars for emperors, then laid down his life grain by grain: the Ganga king Marasimha II, and the last fast at Bankapura.

i18n.hi: जिसने सम्राटों के लिए युद्ध जीते, फिर दाना‑दाना कर प्राण छोड़े: गंगा नरेश मरासिंह द्वितीय और बांकापुर का अंतिम उपवास।

panels.shot: broad aerial view sweeping over the Deccan plateau
panels.action: A bird's-eye view of the Deccan in the 10th century shows scattered walled cities, temple-towns and fortresses on rocky hills, with banners marking the Rashtrakuta capital at Manyakheta and the Ganga lands of Gangavadi to the south.

dialogue.text: In the tenth century, the Deccan was a web of powers: Rashtrakuta emperors at Manyakheta, and their Ganga feudatories guarding Gangavadi in the south.

i18n.hi: दसवीं सदी में दक्कन सत्ता का जाल था: मान्यखेड़ के राष्ट्रकूट सम्राट, और दक्षिण के गंगावाड़ी की रखवाली करते उनके गंगा अधीन राजा।

panels.shot: medium shot inside a palace hall with carved pillars
panels.action: Young Marasimha II stands before an elder court, wearing fine but functional warrior attire, as a court priest gestures toward a map of Gangavadi and the distant Rashtrakuta capital, while armored retainers watch.

dialogue.text: Marasimha, styled Satyavakya, rose in this world as a Ganga prince of Gangavadi, sworn to serve the Rashtrakuta throne yet guarding his own line’s honor.

i18n.hi: सत्यवाक्य मरासिंह, गंगावाड़ी के गंगा कुमार, राष्ट्रकूट सिंहासन की शपथ खाकर भी अपनी कुल‑इज़्ज़त के रखवाले बनकर उभरे।

panels.shot: dynamic battlefield wide shot from behind Marasimha, overlooking troops
panels.action: Marasimha II in full mail, back to the viewer, raises his sword to rally lines of Ganga cavalry and infantry beneath Rashtrakuta umbrella banners, facing a distant fortified town under siege.

dialogue.text: In the reign of Krishna III and later Khottiga, inscriptions remember him in the field, leading Ganga forces for imperial campaigns while holding Gangavadi as a loyal yet forceful feudatory.

i18n.hi: कृष्ण तृतीय और फिर खोट्टिग के समय की शिलालेखों में वे रण में दिखते हैं – गंगा सेना के सेनापति, जो साम्राज्य के लिए लड़ते, पर गंगावाड़ी अपने मज़बूत अधीन राज्य की तरह थामे रखते।

panels.shot: close shot of Marasimha on horseback at dusk
panels.action: Dusty from battle, Marasimha II rides back toward a camp at dusk, his eyes tired; in the distance, a temple spire rises and Jain monks walk in single file, silhouetted against the fading light.

dialogue.text: The same records that praise his campaigns place him in a different light too, as a patron moving among Jain monks and mathas, his name etched later at Shravanabelagola and Bankapura.

i18n.hi: इन्हीं लेखों में वे दूसरी छवि में भी हैं – जैन मुनियों और मठों के बीच घूमते दाता, जिनका नाम बाद में श्रवणबेलगोला और बांकापुर के पत्थरों पर खुदा।

panels.shot: intimate interior medium shot inside a Jain basadi
panels.action: Bareheaded and unarmed, Marasimha II sits on the stone floor of a Jain shrine, hands joined, as a Digambara monk on a low platform speaks calmly, a simple wooden staff resting beside him.

dialogue.speaker: marasimha_ii
dialogue.text: Guru, I have raised forts and burned camps. How does a king unlearn the sword?

i18n.hi: गुरुदेव, मैंने किले उठाए, शिविर जलाए। राजा तलवार भूलना कैसे सीखे?

panels.shot: slow push-in close-up on Marasimha's face lit by oil lamps
panels.action: Marasimha II’s face is lit by flickering lamp light inside the shrine, his features lined, as his gaze shifts from a mural of a meditating Jina to his own calloused hands resting in his lap.

dialogue.text: By the 960s, his world tightened. The Rashtrakuta empire itself was fraying; feudatories like him bore both the weight of imperial wars and their own house’s fate.

i18n.hi: नौ सौ साठ के दशक तक उसकी दुनिया कसने लगी। खुद राष्ट्रकूट साम्राज्य बिखरने लगा; ऐसे अधीनों पर ही सम्राटों के युद्ध और अपने घर की किस्मत दोनों का बोझ था।

panels.shot: wide shot of a fortified town identified through architecture as Bankapura
panels.action: A stout stone fort with high walls and a gate-tower rises over a bustling settlement; within, a Jain temple with a high shikhara stands near the fort walls, flags fluttering in the wind.

dialogue.text: Among the forts tied to his name was Bankapura in today’s Karnataka, later remembered in inscriptions as the place of his final vow.

i18n.hi: उससे जुड़े किलों में एक था आज के कर्नाटक का बांकापुर, जिसे बाद के लेखों ने उसके अंतिम व्रत की धरती कहा।

panels.shot: medium shot in a palace chamber with attendants, from a slightly high angle
panels.action: In a quiet chamber within Bankapura fort, Marasimha II sits on a low throne, removing his jeweled ornaments and passing his sword to a trusted attendant who kneels, eyes lowered.

dialogue.text: At some point near the end of his career, the king laid these burdens down. The Bankapura record speaks of Marasimha undertaking sallekhana, the Jain fast unto death, under monastic guidance.

i18n.hi: राज्य के अंत की ओर किसी मोड़ पर उसने ये बोझ उतार दिए। बांकापुर शिलालेख बताता है, मरासिंह ने जैन संन्यासियों की दीक्षा में सल्लेखना – मृत्यु तक उपवास – धारण किया।

panels.shot: solemn interior wide shot of a Jain hall prepared for vows
panels.action: Inside a simple, clean hall of the Jain temple, Marasimha II now wears plain white cloth, seated cross-legged before a Digambara monk and a small group of lay followers; a stone platform is spread with kusa grass.

dialogue.text: Sallekhana, described in Jain texts and studied by modern scholars, was a gradual, vowed thinning of the body, meant as a conscious exit, not a sudden flight from grief or defeat.

i18n.hi: जैन ग्रंथों और आधुनिक विद्वानों के अनुसार सल्लेखना धीरे‑धीरे देह घटाने का व्रत था – सजग विदाई, न कि अचानक शोक या हार से भागना।

panels.shot: closer side-view of the vow-taking moment
panels.action: Marasimha II touches his folded hands to his forehead, eyes closed, as the monk raises his palm in blessing; attendants stand back, their faces a mix of pride and unease.

dialogue.speaker: marasimha_ii
dialogue.text: As I leave each grain, may I leave each bond of anger and pride.

i18n.hi: जिस तरह हर दाना छोड़ूँ, उसी तरह हर बाँधन – क्रोध, अभिमान – छोड़ सकूँ।

panels.shot: montage-style medium shot showing subtle progression over time
panels.action: In a fixed view of the same hall, Marasimha II sits on the stone platform at different moments: first with a simple meal beside him, later with only water, later with nothing, his frame visibly thinner but his posture still upright.

dialogue.text: The fast unfolded step by measured step. Food reduced, then water, as discipline and weakness wrestled in a body once trained for war.

i18n.hi: उपवास ठहर‑ठहर कर बढ़ा। पहले अन्न घटा, फिर जल; अनुशासन और निर्बलता, युद्ध के लिए पके शरीर में, आमने‑सामने खड़े हुए।

panels.shot: gentle close-up on Marasimha's hand and face
panels.action: A close view shows Marasimha II’s veined hand resting lightly on his knee, fingers relaxed in a meditative gesture, while his face, now gaunt, shows a faint, inward-looking half-smile.

dialogue.text: Inscriptions from Shravanabelagola to Bankapura praise such deaths as heroic restraint, though the wider world, even then, may not always have agreed in silence.

i18n.hi: श्रवणबेलगोला से बांकापुर तक के लेख ऐसे निधन को वीर संयम कहते हैं, भले बाहर की दुनिया तब भी हर बार चुपचाप सहमत न रही हो।

panels.shot: low, reverent shot from the feet of the seated king, looking up past him to the monk
panels.action: Seen from floor level, Marasimha II sits very still on the platform as the monk watches quietly from a short distance; a doorway frames the bright sky beyond, suggesting time passing.

dialogue.text: Modern debates ask whether such fasts can ever be wholly free, or wholly gentle, yet the stone records at Bankapura speak from the side of those who honored his choice.

i18n.hi: आज भी बहस है कि ऐसे उपवास कितने पूरी तरह स्वैच्छिक, कितने सचमुच कोमल; पर बांकापुर के पत्थर तो बस उन लोगों की तरफ से बोलते हैं जिन्होंने उसके निर्णय को सम्मान दिया।

panels.shot: close, detailed shot of a stone inscription surface
panels.action: The panel focuses on a weathered Kannada inscription carved into a stone slab, its letters sharp in some places and eroded in others, while faint shadows from temple pillars fall across the surface.

dialogue.text: Their language is formal and spare: it names the king, notes his vow, locates it at Bankapura, and folds his passing into a lineage of Jain patrons and warrior-ascetics.

i18n.hi: उनकी भाषा सीधी और संक्षिप्त है: राजा का नाम, उसका व्रत, बांकापुर का उल्लेख, और उसका अंत जैन दानियों व योद्धा‑संन्यासियों की परंपरा में जोड़ देना।

panels.shot: soft wide shot showing the final moment in serene abstraction
panels.action: In a quiet, almost abstract scene, Marasimha II sits motionless on the platform, barely more than a silhouette, as lamplight fades and the monk bows his head, the rest of the hall empty and still.

dialogue.text: So ends the trace in stone: the king of Gangavadi, who once rode for Rashtrakutas, is last seen not in battle, but in a hall of silence at Bankapura.

i18n.hi: यहीं पत्थर पर आख़िरी छाप बचती है: गंगावाड़ी का राजा, जो कभी राष्ट्रकूटों के लिए घुड़ता था, आख़िर में रण में नहीं, बांकापुर की निःशब्द दीक्षा‑सभामें दिखता है।

panels.shot: modern-day wide shot of Shravanabelagola hill from a distance
panels.action: From afar, the great hill of Shravanabelagola rises with the colossus of Gommateshvara barely visible, while visitors climb the steps below and a scholar stands looking up, notebook in hand.

dialogue.text: Today, at Shravanabelagola and other sites, historians read such epigraphs alongside Jain texts, weighing praise against pain, devotion against power, in trying to understand lives like Marasimha’s.

i18n.hi: आज श्रवणबेलगोला और और जगहों पर इतिहासकार ऐसे शिलालेखों को जैन ग्रंथों के साथ रखकर पढ़ते हैं – जहाँ स्तुति के साथ पीड़ा, भक्ति के साथ सत्ता भी तौलते हुए मरासिंह जैसे जीवन समझने की कोशिश है।

panels.shot: reflective medium-wide shot of an empty throne and a bare stone platform side by side
panels.action: In a symbolic composition, an ornate empty throne stands in one half of the frame within a dim palace hall, while in the other half a bare stone platform sits under open sky, both deserted yet inviting the viewer’s gaze.

dialogue.text: His story endures as a hard question rather than an easy lesson: how a single life in medieval Karnataka could hold both the sword of a Rashtrakuta general and the slow, deliberate renunciation of sallekhana.

i18n.hi: उसकी कथा आसान शिक्षा नहीं, कठिन सवाल बनकर बची है: कैसे मध्यकालीन कर्नाटक का एक जीवन राष्ट्रकूट सेनापति की तलवार और सल्लेखना की धीमी, सोची‑समझी विरक्ति – दोनों को एक साथ थाम सकता था।

subtitle_i18n.en: A feudatory king between sword and silence
subtitle_i18n.hi: तलवार और मौन के बीच फँसा अधीन राजा
